module_title: Constitutional Conflicts, Harmonious Construction & Basic Structure
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the intense historical and judicial warfare between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs, culminating in the Doctrine of Harmonious Construction and the Basic Structure Doctrine.

core_concepts.title: The Conflict: FRs vs. DPSPs
core_concepts.description:
What happens when a law made to implement a DPSP violates an FR? 
- Phase 1: Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951) ruled that FRs are superior, and DPSPs run subsidiary to them.
- Phase 2: 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Art 31C, protecting laws implementing DPSPs 39(b) & (c) from being challenged under Arts 14, 19, or 31.
- Phase 3: 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to give primacy to ALL DPSPs over FRs 14, 19, and 31.

core_concepts.title: Minerva Mills Case (1980): The Truce
core_concepts.description:
The Supreme Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's blanket primacy to DPSPs. 
- The Court established the Doctrine of Harmonious Construction: The Indian Constitution is founded on the **bedrock of the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles**. 
- Giving absolute primacy to one over the other is like destroying the structure. They are like two wheels of a chariot. Laws implementing DPSPs 39(b) and (c) are protected against Arts 14 and 19, but beyond that, the balance must be maintained.

core_concepts.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
core_concepts.description:
Established in the landmark *Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala (1973)*. 
- Rule: Parliament can amend ANY part of the Constitution under Article 368 (including Fundamental Rights), PROVIDED it does not alter or destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution. 
- The balance between FRs and DPSPs, Secularism, Judicial Review, and the Rule of Law are all parts of the Basic Structure.

core_concepts.title: Enforceability of Fundamental Duties
core_concepts.description: Though non-justiciable, courts use FDs to interpret laws. In *M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (1988)*, the Supreme Court invoked Art 51A(g) (duty to protect the natural environment) to make environmental education compulsory in schools and colleges. FDs act as a warning to citizens that while enjoying their rights, they must be conscious of their obligations.

important_entities.name: Article 31C
important_entities.significance: Inserted to protect laws aimed at securing the equitable distribution of material resources (39b) and preventing the concentration of wealth (39c). If a law serves these two DPSPs, it cannot be struck down merely because it violates the Right to Equality (Art 14) or Freedom (Art 19).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams often ask which case stated that Parliament has NO power to amend Fundamental Rights. The answer is the **Golaknath Case (1967)**. However, remember this was OVERRULED six years later by the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), which restored the amending power subject to the Basic Structure.

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Timeline of the FR vs DPSP War
mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: C G K M (Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: C (1951: FRs win) -> G (1967: FRs unamendable) -> K (1973: Amendable but Basic Structure limits it) -> M (1980: Balance is the Basic Structure).

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains or Law Optionals, when answering a question on the relationship between FRs and DPSPs, ALWAYS conclude with the 'Bedrock of Balance' analogy from the Minerva Mills case.
